title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: After saying goodbye to her guests, Anna did not sit down but started pacing up and down the room. She had, without quite meaning to, spent the whole evening doing her utmost to spark a feeling of love in Levin—as lately she had been doing with all young men—and she knew she had managed it, as far as one can in a single evening with a married and conscientious man. She did like him a great deal, and despite the striking difference between Vronsky and Levin from a man's point of view, as a woman she could see something they had in common, something that had made it possible for Kitty to love both of them. Yet as soon as he was out of the room, she stopped thinking about him.

One thought, and only one, kept chasing her in different forms, and would not leave her alone. "If I can have so much effect on others—on this man, who loves his home and his wife—why is _he_ so cold to me?... not cold, exactly, he loves me, I know that! But something new is pulling us apart now. Why wasn't he here all evening? He sent word through Stiva that he couldn't leave Yashvin and had to watch over his play. Is Yashvin a child? But suppose it's true. He never lies. But if it's true, there's something else in it. He's glad of a chance to show me he has other duties; I know that, I accept that. But why does he have to prove it to me? He wants to show me that his love for me isn't going to interfere with his freedom. But I don't need proofs—I need love. He ought to understand how bitter this life is for me here in Moscow. Is this a life? I'm not living, I'm waiting for something that keeps being put off and put off. Still no answer! And Stiva says he can't go to Alexey Alexandrovitch. And I can't write again. I can do nothing, start nothing, change nothing. I hold myself in, I wait, inventing amusements—the English family, my writing, reading—but it's all a sham, it's all the same as morphine. He ought to feel for me," she said, feeling tears of self-pity rising in her eyes.

She heard Vronsky's abrupt ring and quickly dried her tears—not only dried them, but sat down by a lamp and opened a book, putting on an air of composure. She wanted him to see that she was annoyed he hadn't come home when he promised—just annoyed, and on no account to let him see her distress, least of all her self-pity. She might pity herself, but he must not pity her. She didn't want a quarrel, she blamed him for wanting one, but without realizing it, she settled into a stance of attack.
"Well, you weren't bored?" he said, eagerly and good-humoredly, as he came up to her. "What a terrible passion it is—gambling!"
"No, I wasn't bored; I learned long ago how not to be bored. Stiva was here, and Levin."
"Yes, they meant to come and see you. Well, how did you like Levin?" he said, sitting down beside her.
"Very much. They haven't long been gone. What was Yashvin doing?"
"He was winning—seventeen thousand. I got him to leave. He'd actually started for home, but then he turned around, and now he's losing."

"Then why did you stay?" she asked, suddenly lifting her eyes to him. The expression on her face was cold and ungracious. "You told Stiva you were staying to get Yashvin away. And you left him there."
The same expression of cold readiness for a fight came over his face too.

"In the first place, I didn't ask him to bring you any message; and second, I never lie. But what matters most is that I wanted to stay, and I stayed," he said, frowning. "Anna, what is this for, why are you doing this?" he said after a moment's silence, leaning toward her and opening his hand, hoping she would put hers in it.
She was glad of this appeal for tenderness. But some strange, evil force would not let her give in to her feelings, as though the rules of war would not let her surrender.

"Of course you wanted to stay, and you stayed. You do whatever you want. But why are you telling me that? What for?" she said, growing more and more agitated. "Is anyone disputing your rights? But you want to be right, and by all means be right."
His hand closed, he turned away, and his face took on an even more stubborn expression.

"For you it's a matter of stubbornness," she said, watching him intently and suddenly hitting on the right word for the look that irritated her, "simple stubbornness. For you it's a question of whether you keep the upper hand of me, and for me...." Again she felt sorry for herself, and almost burst into tears. "If you knew what this is for me! When I feel, as I do now, that you are hostile—yes, hostile to me—if you knew what that means for me! If you knew how I feel on the brink of disaster at this very moment, how afraid I am of myself!" And she turned away, hiding her sobs.

"But what are you talking about?" he said, horrified at her look of despair, and bending over her again, he took her hand and kissed it. "What is it for? Am I looking for amusements outside our home? Don't I avoid the company of women?"
"Well, yes! If only that were all!" she said.

"Come, tell me what I ought to do to give you peace of mind? I'm ready to do anything to make you happy," he said, moved by her look of despair; "what wouldn't I do to spare you any distress, as now, Anna!" he said.

"It's nothing, nothing!" she said. "I don't know myself whether it's the loneliness, my nerves.... Come, let's not talk about it. What about the race? You haven't told me!" she asked, trying to hide her triumph at the victory which, in the end, had been hers.

He asked for supper and began telling her about the races; but in his voice, in his eyes, which grew colder and colder, she saw he did not forgive her her victory, that the stubborn streak she had been fighting had reasserted itself in him. He was cooler with her than before, as though he regretted having given in. And she, remembering the words that had won her the victory—"how I feel on the brink of disaster, how afraid I am of myself"—saw that this was a dangerous weapon, and that she could not use it a second time. And she felt that alongside the love that bound them together, there had grown up some evil spirit of conflict between them, one she could not drive out of his heart, and still less out of her own.
